title: Sony Music and Warner Chappell sue Anthropic over song-lyric training data
subtitle: The publishers seek up to $150,000 per work — potentially billions — accusing Anthropic of torrenting and scraping tens of thousands of compositions to train Claude.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music filed a joint complaint against Anthropic in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleging what the publishers call 'one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history.' The complaint names Anthropic co-founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann as individual defendants and asks for statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work, plus up to $25,000 for each instance where copyright-management information was stripped — a range that could total several billion dollars if maximized.

The mechanism the publishers describe is specific: they allege Anthropic pulled compositions and lyrics from torrent networks including Library Genesis and Pirate Library Mirror, and separately scraped lyric-database sites Musixmatch and LyricFind. Torrenting is the legally dangerous verb here — unlike a good-faith scrape of a public web page, downloading a torrent seed is itself an act of distribution under U.S. copyright law, which is why the plaintiffs are calling out that specific ingestion path rather than the training step alone.

Anthropic already settled the largest AI copyright case on record — a $1.5 billion agreement with book authors approved in July 2026, after Judge Alsup's split ruling found the training use itself was fair but the acquisition-by-torrent was not. That precedent is the pattern Sony and Warner are now trying to apply to music. A parallel record-labels case against Suno and Udio, filed by RIAA members in 2024, has been in discovery for two years and reached a partial verdict in Germany in July; the U.S. music-publishing side has been waiting for the right AI-lab defendant with a fresh precedent to lean on. The Bartz settlement gave them one.

For learners: the interesting line here is not 'is training on copyrighted data legal' — that is still contested and jurisdiction-dependent. The line is 'how did the data get onto your training cluster.' A model trained on a licensed corpus, or on a public-web crawl that respects robots.txt, is a very different legal exposure than one trained on a torrent of pirated books or a scrape that bypassed a paywall. If you are building on any model, that provenance chain is now a material risk your legal team will ask about.
